message.content:
You work in the Fortress revival at /home/user/fortress, for its coordinating session. Load the `fortress-repo` skill's core (.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md) and its references/records.md, then the `coordinator` skill's core (.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md), its references/record.md whole (the record's tools, "The pass", "A consolidation", "The consolidation tools"), references/batch.md's section "The landing", and the manual explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md's section "After the landing: the coordinator's routing".

The problem. After each batch of the compile ladder lands, the record (FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, their history files, INDEX.md, PLAN.md, PLAN-history.md, review-queue.md and the gap ledger, all under explorations/coordinator/ and explorations/) must be brought in line with what landed: the pass over the entries the batch added or changed, the POSITIONS sentences the tree made false, the routing of the batch's items and PLAN's moves, the orientation of the worker skill. Today the coordinating session does this by hand, with several workers briefed one by one. At climb batch 24's landing on 2026-10-31 it took: a post-batch review (commit 43cd61b62), the orientation workflow in update mode (explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/, commit 6d4e58a3b), a record writer for FACTS and POSITIONS (be3b07aac, 08cc69e2d), a routing worker for PLAN, PLAN-history, the review queue and INDEX (b49631cb4, 85b2998e9), a skill writer in four tasks and a cold read, and a worker for the workflow's own fixes (7abc5c21c). The curator, who directs this project, wants the record's part of this to be one reusable workflow that the coordinator launches after a landing, so that the coordinator does not read the whole record and brief each step itself. His words, dictated, on the drafts of two skill rules about it:

"I wanted to have the process encoded in the workflow. So parts of it go into the coordinator skill. But [...] part of this update should be ensuring that like a workflow can support the described process, and that the coordinator doesn't have to do it manually. So what I'm not sure is this a new process that has Clarity workflow as part of it, or like, does a coordinator need to read everything, or can it just get the workflow that prepares a diff, and then coordinator just sees the diff in the skill and is aware what changed to update its context, and we just go on from there? Maybe I am concerned with wrong kinds of efficiency. This is simply the cost that the coordinator must pay."

"Is Clarity workflow the correct tool to use for consolidating the record after the batch lands? I believe we had some success in using this manually when we tried to encode this, but [...] we had issues with reusing the workflow last time. You needed to modify the script to allow for it to take a different input structure, I believe. So I'm unsure we got this correctly worded here. And I would hate to create an issue by encoding this incorrectly. So can we measure twice here before we cut? But ideally the goal here would be to get the new facts and stuff from, I believe, from a report of the landed batch is also considered an input. Like maybe there is a step that gathers the evidence for the consolidation of the record that is like what those scouts prepared for each chunk. And then Opus writer consolidated. I'm not really sure what the right form is, but I'd like to have this down to a reusable workflow after the batch lands that the coordinator launches, and we get a consistent record keeping consolidation. [...] This sounds like something not for a tool writer, but for a dedicated worker to examine what I am blabbering about and how to encode the successful part of the process into something that can be just launched by the coordinator after the batch lands without it needing to do a lot of reading of the records and correcting, gathering evidence. Like, that part should be encoded in the workflow. And also the writing. Like, we had the writer process in batches, etc., etc. So, that part was in the workflow. Like, we have a headless writer that keeps the register in ASD ST100, and we had that process that writes the position with its history or fact history. Like, that part should be encoded in the workflow and reused. And I believe we had a success in using this, but when I tried it from such vague instructions, it backfired, so I don't know where the gap was."

He also said of the consolidation's scope: it covers the whole record, FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX alike, not FACTS alone; consolidating the record is the coordinator's job, which it may delegate, so that the batch's workers keep their record-keeping short.

The question. Examine, then design; build nothing yet ("measure twice"). Write a design note that answers:
1. What exists. The clarity workflow (explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/, its README and scripts, its headless Opus writer stream writer-stream.sh that keeps the ASD-STE100 register and writes through record.py with the history), the ledger-clarity run (tools/ledger-clarity/), the orientation workflow's update mode (tools/orientation/, a model of "admit the landing's entries, write, check, judge"), and the batch script's commit stage, which already folds each rung's record.md and the gate's figures (explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js, its commit stage). What each takes as input, what it writes, what it checks. Where the clarity workflow was reused with a different input and had to be changed: read its git history (`git log --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/`) and the notes INDEX.md lists for it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'index:clarity'`), and say what the gap was.
2. What the landing's record work is, step by step, from today's commits (read each: `git show --stat` and the diffs of be3b07aac, 08cc69e2d, b49631cb4, 85b2998e9, and the review's Part 4 in explorations/reviews/batch-24-review.md) and from climb batch 23's (`git log --oneline 3cd653815..f2714393a`): which steps are mechanical (diff the record against the base, list the changed entries, run record.py check and ledger.py landing-check, the "Needed by" of a queue item), which need an Opus writer's judgement (the pass's wording, a POSITIONS sentence made false, a PLAN line moved as built), and which need the coordinator or the curator (a decision, a default).
3. The design: one workflow the coordinator launches after a landing with the base and the landing commit as arguments. Its stages, in the pattern of orientation.js: an evidence stage that gathers what the writer needs (the record's diff, the batch's RECORD.md, the review's findings on the record, the ledger's changed rows, the POSITIONS sentences that cite changed rows or entries), a writer stage by the headless Opus stream through record.py, checks (record.py check, ledger.py check, a cold read of the changed entries, the routing check), a fix round, and a judge that hands the coordinator a diff with one line per change. Say what the coordinator still reads (the diff and the judge's lines) and what it no longer reads. Say whether the clarity workflow is the base to extend (a new mode) or the writer stream alone is reused, and why. Give the inputs, outputs and the checks of each stage, the model of each agent, and a cost estimate in tokens written from today's workers (the batch-24 review's section 3 gives the method). Name the risks: a writer that changes a decision's meaning, a step that needs the curator's word, a change to the record that the batch's own commit stage already made.
4. What stays with the coordinator, and the smallest first version worth building.

Where the sources are. The record's tools and their READMEs under explorations/coordinator/tools/; the notes INDEX.md lists for "clarity", "consolidation", "orientation" and "landing" (`facts-extract.sh 'index:WORD'`); the batch-24 review's Part 4 and section 3; the commits named above; explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/ (the folder of such notes; batch-redesign.md and plan-map.md are models of the form).

Rules. Read only; run only the scripts' help or dry runs that write nothing, and git. Write the note to explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md with a header comment in the folder's form, and add its INDEX line to explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md in the file's form and place. Commit the two by named paths (`git add -- <new file>`, then `git commit -m ... -- <paths>`) with the trailer lines `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>` and `Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB`; push nothing; if git reports an index lock, wait ten seconds and try again (other writers commit in this tree). Write halfway to ASD-STE100: plain short sentences, one word for one thing, lists not tables where a phone reads them. End with a report: the design in ten lines, the decisions for the curator (each with a default), the smallest first version and its cost, and the commit.

# Fortress revival

Fortress was an experimental programming language from Sun Labs (2003–2012).
This repository revives it: the goal is to finish the original team's design,
judged by its specification (`Specification/`) and its type research
(`Papers/`), and measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and
running fast.

## Where your training applies, and where it does not

- Known languages: the interpreter, the code generator and the run time are
  Java (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`); the static type checker is
  Scala (`.../scala_src/`); the parser grammars are Rats! (`.../parser/*.rats`);
  the syntax tree is generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`; the
  build is Ant; the specification and the papers are LaTeX.
- Fortress itself: the library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`),
  the tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and the other test
  folders) and every `.fss` and `.fsi` file. Fortress is not in your training
  in any depth. It looks like Scala in places, and its library's algebraic
  traits recall Haskell's numeric classes, but its rules differ (multiple
  dispatch, juxtaposition as an operator, loops parallel by default), so
  assuming it behaves like a language you know can lead you astray.

## How to work here

- Before any build, test run, edit, measurement, commit or agent launch, load
  the `fortress-repo` skill, which also covers long commands and waits; for
  the cloud container's machine, disk, stops and restarts, and a lost
  container, the `cloud-container` skill.
- The coordinating session loads the `fortress-repo` skill, then the
  `coordinator` skill, at session start and after every compaction, and boots
  and works by the `coordinator` skill, which also covers running agents and
  resuming runs.

1	---
2	name: fortress-repo
3	description: "Use this skill whenever you touch the code of the Fortress language revival (/home/user/fortress or a worktree like fortress-w4): building with ant; recompiling after editing a .fss, .fsi, Java or Scala file; running programs under walk or the bytecode compiler; running or writing tests (testFast, testSystem, harness-one.sh, junit.sh, .test files, XXX expected failures); the gate before landing; editing the interpreter, compiled checker, code generator, Library or Specification; searching the gap ledger or git history; seeding worktrees; committing a code change. Load it before even a small build, test, edit or measurement there, including long background runs you wait on, and when briefing agents for that work; then read references/revival-changes.md whole before work. Skip it for session upkeep (compaction, boot notes, reading batch results, scheduling agents: coordinator skill, read after this file), Stop hooks, disk or container trouble (cloud-container), other repos, and general Fortress history."
4	---
5	
6	# Working in the Fortress revival repository
7	
8	The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.
9	
10	**curator**
11	: Person in charge of this restoration.
12	
13	**brief**
14	: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.
15	
16	**original tree**
17	: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.
18	
19	**record**
20	: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).
21	
22	**walk**
23	: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.
24	
25	**compiled path**
26	: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.
27	
28	**model program**
29	: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.
30	
31	**one library**
32	: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).
33	
34	**component**
35	: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.
36	
37	**api**
38	: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.
39	
40	**area**
41	: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the run time), the library, or the specification.
42	
43	**base**
44	: Commit that your work starts from.
45	
46	**gate**
47	: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.
48	
49	**harness**
50	: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.
51	
52	**building**
53	: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.
54	
55	**exploring**
56	: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.
57	
58	You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.
59	
60	## How a program runs
61	
62	Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.
63	
64	### The phases
65	
66	Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):
67	
68	1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
69	2. Bind each name to its declaration.
70	3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
71	4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
72	5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
73	6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.
74	
75	Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.
76	
77	`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.
78	
79	Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.
80	
81	### The compiled run time
82	
83	`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:
84	
85	- the component's functions, objects and traits;
86	- its closures;
87	- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.
88	
89	A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.
90	
91	The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
92	
93	HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.
94	
95	### The caches
96	
97	A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.
98	
99	- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
100	- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
101	- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
102	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.
103	
104	In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).
105	
106	`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.
107	
108	### Parallelism and mutable state
109	
110	Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.
111	
112	`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A `value` object has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`.
113	
114	Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:
115	
116	- Most data is immutable.
117	- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
118	- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
119	- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").
120	
121	So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.
122	
123	Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).
124	
125	## Fortress as a language
126	
127	Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.
128	
129	- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
130	- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
131	- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
132	- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
133	- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
134	- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
135	- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
136	- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).
137	
138	## The record
139	
140	The record's main files:
141	
142	- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
143	- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
144	- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
145	- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.
146	
147	Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.
148	
149	## When to explore
150	
151	Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:
152	
153	- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
154	- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
155	- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.
156	
157	When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.
158	
159	## Rules for every task
160	
161	- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
162	- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
163	- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
164	- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
165	- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
166	- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
167	- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
168	- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
169	- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
170	- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
171	- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
172	- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
173	- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
174	- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
175	- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
176	- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
177	- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch: logs, captured output, probe programs. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. Each agent's transcript keeps how the work was done (`references/committing.md`).
178	- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).
179	
180	## The parts
181	
182	Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.
183	
184	The parts, in the order that work meets them:
185	
186	- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
187	- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
188	- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
189	- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
190	- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
191	- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the run time, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
192	- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
193	- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
194	- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know; read it whole, after this file, before work: `references/revival-changes.md`
195	- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
196	- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
197	- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
198	- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
199	- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
200	- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
201	- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.
202	
203	A task usually needs several parts, and every task needs `revival-changes.md`, read whole before work, and `records.md`, for its queries and its report. For example, a fix of walk needs `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.
204	
205	`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
117	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
118	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
119
